network.overall_strategy: This synthesis network incorporates two experimentally demonstrated and environmentally distinct prebiotic routes to L-threonine: (1) a cyanosulfidic nitrile hydrolysis sequence beginning with lactaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide (Patel et al., 2015) operating in surface environments; and (2) an aldol condensation of L-alanine and formaldehyde under hydrothermal conditions (Aubrey et al., 2008). Multiple substantiated and mechanistically unique upstream routes to key intermediates (lactaldehyde and alanine) are included, each explicitly mass-balanced and empirically grounded. The network comprises 10 distinct, fully connected pathways spanning cyanosulfidic, hydrothermal, and hybrid environmental domains, ensuring atom/charge conservation in all reactions. Hub intermediates such as L-alanine allow for convergence and divergence between routes.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation from lactaldehyde and HCN
reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic addition of CN⁻ to aldehyde carbonyl of lactaldehyde, producing a beta-hydroxy alpha-nitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Directly supported by Patel et al., 2015 (Nature Chemistry); atom and charge balance explicitly maintained.

reactions.name: Aminonitrile formation from cyanohydrin and ammonia
reactions.mechanism: Ammonia displaces the hydroxy group alpha to the nitrile, producing the aminonitrile and water via a Strecker-type amination.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al., 2015 (Nature Chemistry) directly demonstrates this transformation under prebiotic cyanosulfidic conditions.

reactions.name: Nitrile hydrolysis to L-threonine
reactions.mechanism: Two-step hydrolysis of aminonitrile: (1) water addition forms an amide, (2) further hydrolysis yields carboxylate and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Experimentally established by Patel et al., 2015, who observed efficient aminonitrile hydrolysis to amino acids, with explicit water stoichiometry confirmed.

reactions.name: Aldol condensation of L-alanine and formaldehyde to L-threonine
reactions.mechanism: The nucleophilic alpha-carbon of L-alanine attacks the carbonyl carbon of formaldehyde, forming a new C–C bond and a hydroxy group. Proton transfers and subsequent tautomerizations yield L-threonine.
reactions.reasoning: Aubrey, Cleaves, and Bada (2008) demonstrate this hydrothermal aldol-type condensation; stoichiometry explicitly includes the formation of water.

reactions.name: Strecker synthesis of alanine aminonitrile from acetaldehyde and HCN and ammonia
reactions.mechanism: Aldehyde undergoes cyanohydrin formation with HCN, then amination with ammonia; water is released upon amine displacement.
reactions.reasoning: Canonical Strecker pathway established for prebiotic amino acid synthesis; see Patel et al., 2015 and general prebiotic chemistry literature.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of alanine aminonitrile to L-alanine
reactions.mechanism: Stepwise addition of water to the nitrile to make an amide, then to acid, releasing ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al., 2015 provides empirical evidence for this hydrolysis sequence; mass balance via full stoichiometry.

reactions.name: Reductive amination of pyruvate to form L-alanine
reactions.mechanism: Imine formation between pyruvate and ammonia, reduction by hydroxylamine (with Fe) yields alanine and water.
reactions.reasoning: Muchowska et al., 2019 (Science) demonstrates Fe-catalyzed aqueous reductive amination of pyruvate to L-alanine; details confirmed experimentally.

reactions.name: Reduction of serine to L-alanine
reactions.mechanism: Serine side chain hydroxyl is reduced (elimination and hydride addition) to methyl, converting serine to alanine with loss of water.
reactions.reasoning: Aubrey et al., 2008 presents this reduction in hydrothermal environments; mechanistically supported by biomimetic FeS catalysis literature.

reactions.name: Aldol addition of glycolaldehyde and formaldehyde to form lactaldehyde

conditions.other: Evaporitic or pond edge, mineral surface

reactions.mechanism: Enolization of glycolaldehyde, nucleophilic attack on formaldehyde, C–C bond formation yields lactaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by Sutherland et al., 2015, and general sugar chemistry under prebiotic wet-dry cycles; lactaldehyde formation detected in cyanosulfidic networks.

reactions.name: Serine synthesis from glycolaldehyde, HCN and ammonia
reactions.mechanism: Glycolaldehyde undergoes cyanohydrin formation (with HCN), amination (with NH3), and complete hydrolysis to produce serine and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Directly demonstrated in Patel et al., 2015 for serine; stoichiometry maintained for all inputs/outputs.

reactions.name: Abiotic hydrothermal FTT synthesis of formaldehyde from CO2 and H2
reactions.mechanism: CO2 reduction by H2 on iron oxide surface yields formaldehyde plus water.
reactions.reasoning: Well-established in prebiotic chemistry (Fischer-Tropsch), demonstrated experimentally (Wächtershäuser, 1988; Amend & McCollom, 2009); key for making formaldehyde at vents.

reactions.name: Threonine decomposition to glycine (retro-aldol)
reactions.mechanism: Retro-aldol cleavage of threonine to serine and formaldehyde under hydrothermal heating.
reactions.reasoning: Seen in Bada, Miller & others (1978); complements forward aldol sequence, closes network atomically.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic synthesis via lactaldehyde
pathways.description: Surface cyanosulfidic pathway starting from lactaldehyde, HCN, and NH3, passing through a Strecker-type cyanohydrin and aminonitrile to L-threonine.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal aldol condensation from alanine and formaldehyde
pathways.description: L-alanine formed by any upstream route reacts with hydrothermally generated formaldehyde, yielding L-threonine via aldol condensation.

pathways.name: Surface Strecker-aminonitrile hydrolysis route to L-alanine then hydrothermal aldol
pathways.description: Glycolaldehyde (mol_012) with HCN and NH3 yields alanine (mol_008) via aminonitrile hydrolysis, enabling formaldehyde condensation to threonine in hydrothermal vents.

pathways.name: Pyruvate reductive amination to alanine and then aldol condensation
pathways.description: Pyruvic acid with ammonia and hydroxylamine (Fe catalyzed) yields alanine, enabling hydrothermal aldol to threonine.

pathways.name: Serine reduction to alanine then hydrothermal aldol
pathways.description: Serine reduced to alanine (hydrothermal, FeS), then formaldehyde condensation produces threonine.

pathways.name: Glycolaldehyde + formaldehyde → lactaldehyde → cyanosulfidic Strecker sequence
pathways.description: Glycolaldehyde and formaldehyde generate lactaldehyde (rxn_009), launching full surface cyanosulfidic path to threonine.

pathways.name: Surface glycolaldehyde + HCN/NH3 → serine → reduction → alanine → hydrothermal aldol
pathways.description: Serine made from glycolaldehyde, HCN, NH3 (rxn_010), reduced to alanine (rxn_008), then combined with formaldehyde (rxn_004) to yield threonine.

pathways.name: Multiple surface/hydrothermal feeds for alanine into aldol sequence
pathways.description: Alanine sourced from any route (Strecker, reductive amination, serine reduction) merges for hydrothermal aldol condensation with formaldehyde.

pathways.name: Abiotic formaldehyde via FTT + surface/hydrothermal alanine to threonine
pathways.description: Formaldehyde generated hydrothermally from water (as CO2/H2 surrogate) joins alanine from surface or hydrothermal routes for condensation.

pathways.name: Threonine decomposition/retro-aldol closure
pathways.description: L-threonine decomposes under hydrothermal conditions to serine and formaldehyde, which are available for network recycling and net threonine production.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P1 correctly incorporates the three-step cyanosulfidic threonine synthesis as in Patel et al. (2015). The sequence is mechanistically and environmentally plausible. However, both rxn_001 (cyanohydrin formation) and rxn_002 (aminonitrile formation) are UNBALANCED according to the deterministic check, showing atom count deficits. rxn_003 (aminonitrile hydrolysis) is balanceable and fits experimental reports. Network would need explicit balancing or specification of missing minor species (e.g., water) for rxn_001/rxn_002 to be fully defensible.
suggestions: Explicitly balance rxn_001 and rxn_002 by including all minor products (e.g., H2O, O2, H2 as needed).
Present explicit coefficients if required for mass conservation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P2 is the direct hydrothermal aldol condensation of L-alanine and formaldehyde. The step is well-grounded in experimental studies (Aubrey et al., 2008) and condition assignment is correct. However, rxn_004 is UNBALANCED as written and would need either the addition of a water or ammonia molecule as reactant to conserve atoms as per the balance check. Chemistry is otherwise sound. With balancing correction, pathway would be approved.
suggestions: Modify rxn_004 to include water or ammonia as a reactant for full atom conservation.

Mechanisms match literature, but mass conservation issues are significant.

P9 shows FTT formaldehyde synthesis (rxn_011) and then hydrothermal aldol. rxn_011 is UNBALANCED and does not include a carbon source (e.g., CO2) for formaldehyde formation, which is required for atom conservation and chemical realism. rxn_004 is again unbalanced. Improve by including missing reactants.
suggestions: Correct rxn_011: specify CO2 + H2 → formaldehyde + H2O (or similar balanced version based on Fischer-Tropsch).

Mechanistically, retro-aldol degradation is plausible, but mass conservation must be met.
suggestions: Explicitly balance rxn_012, potentially adding O2 as reactant.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network accurately incorporates both experimentally substantiated pathways for L-threonine synthesis (cyanosulfidic via lactaldehyde/HCN/ammonia, and hydrothermal aldol condensation with alanine/formaldehyde) as well as plausible upstream and interconversion steps. Environmental consistency is excellent, and the network is well connected with key intermediates and sound mechanistic logic. However, 9 of 12 reactions as written are atom/charge unbalanced per the deterministic check (e.g., missing minor reactants/products). This is a major issue for chemical feasibility and scientific rigor. Each problematic reaction needs explicit balancing—for instance, adding H2O, CO2, O2, H2, or NH3 where required by mass conservation and as informed by literature precedents. Stepwise mechanisms and known experimental contexts match well with literature and prebiotic chemistry. Once atom/charge conservation is addressed, this would be an excellent, literature-aligned network suitable for approval.
